title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
statement: An array sorted in ascending order was rotated between 1 and n times, so [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] may have become [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]. All elements are distinct. Return the minimum element in O(log n) time.
realWorld: Ring buffers and circular logs. A fixed-size append-only log that wraps around holds timestamps in ascending order except for one wrap point; finding the oldest surviving record means finding exactly this minimum. The same shape appears when reading a circular journal or a rotated time-series shard and you need to know where the sequence actually begins.

examples.explanation: The original [1,2,3,4,5] was rotated 3 times. The minimum sits at index 3, immediately after the one descending step.
A full rotation leaves the array sorted. There is no descending step, so the answer is nums[0] — the case that breaks any solution that insists on finding a drop.
The smallest interesting input. low = 0, high = 1, mid = 0; nums[0] = 2 > nums[1] = 1, so low becomes 1 and the loop ends.

constraints: The array is a rotation of a strictly ascending array

bruteForce.idea: Scan every element and keep the smallest, or scan for the single position where the value drops.
code: for (int i = 1; i < nums.length; i++) {   // every element, as if the order told us nothing
bruteForce.whySlow: The scan treats the array as unordered and re-derives, element by element, a structure the problem already handed you. Two thirds of every comparison is wasted: one look at a midpoint tells you which half of the array contains the wrap point, and the scan asks n separate questions to learn what log n questions would settle. The array is not sorted, but it is not arbitrary either, and a linear scan is what you pay when you refuse to exploit the difference.

patternIdentification: A rotated sorted array is two ascending runs stuck together, and every element of the left run is larger than every element of the right run. That gives you a monotone predicate — 'is nums[i] in the right (small) run?' is false, false, ..., true, true — and a monotone predicate is all binary search needs. The general move: when an array is not globally sorted but is made of a bounded number of sorted pieces, look for a comparison that tells you which piece the midpoint is in, and binary search on that instead of on the values.

optimized.idea:
Compare nums[mid] against nums[high], not nums[low]. If nums[mid] > nums[high], then mid is in the left (large) run and the wrap point is strictly to its right, so low = mid + 1. Otherwise mid is in the right (small) run and could itself be the minimum, so high = mid. The range shrinks every step and converges on the minimum.

Why nums[high] and not nums[low]? Because the comparison against the low end answers the wrong question. In [3,4,5,1,2] the probe is mid = 2, nums[mid] = 5, nums[low] = 3, so nums[mid] > nums[low] — and the minimum is to the right. In [1,2,3,4,5] the probe is mid = 2, nums[mid] = 3, nums[low] = 1, so nums[mid] > nums[low] again — and the minimum is at index 0, to the left. Identical comparison, opposite conclusions, so nums[low] alone cannot decide which half to keep. Against nums[high] the answer is never ambiguous: nums[mid] > nums[high] holds if and only if mid sits in the left run, because every element of the left run exceeds every element of the right run and nums[high] is always in the right run (or, in the un-rotated case, is the whole array's maximum, so the test is correctly false and the search walks left).

With duplicates allowed (the 'II' variant), nums[mid] == nums[high] tells you nothing — the wrap point could be on either side — and the only safe move is high-- , which degrades the worst case to O(n) on an input like [1,1,1,0,1].
code: low = mid + 1;      // mid is in the left (large) run, so the minimum is strictly right of it
high = mid;         // mid is in the right (small) run and may be the minimum itself

commonMistakes: Comparing nums[mid] with nums[low] instead of nums[high]. It works on [4,5,6,7,0,1,2] and then returns 4 on the un-rotated [1,2,3,4,5], because nums[mid] > nums[low] is true there too but means the opposite thing — the symptom is a wrong answer only on arrays that happen to be fully sorted.

Writing `high = mid - 1` in the else branch. When mid is already the minimum it gets thrown away: on [2,1] mid = 0 is not greater than nums[1], high becomes -1, and you index nums[-1] or return the wrong element. The symptom is an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException on two-element inputs.

Using `while (low <= high)` with `high = mid`. Once low == high == mid the assignment changes nothing and the loop never exits — the test hangs rather than failing, which is easy to misread as a slow machine.
